name: Straw phonation

lead: Straw phonation means making voiced sound while blowing through a narrow straw, which partly closes the vocal tract. People use it as a warm-up and drill for a clearer, more controlled voice.

It belongs to the semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) family of exercises used by voice teachers and speech-language pathologists. Narrowing the opening changes air pressure and airflow at the vocal folds, and imaging and aerodynamic studies in singers have measured changes in vocal tract shape and glottal function. Studies in singers and people with voice disorders are mostly short-term and small, and none addresses perceived attractiveness.

paras: People hum or glide in pitch through a straw for a few minutes as a warm-up or cool-down, often in short daily sessions, and then speak or sing with the same easy feel. Voice-improvement communities have adopted it alongside other warm-ups.
The reviewed studies report no notable harms. People with a voice disorder are generally directed by clinicians to a speech-language pathologist.

angle.text: Voicing through a straw is used to get a clearer, steadier, more controlled voice. The narrowed opening eases phonation at the vocal folds. It is an established SOVT exercise with clinical research on voice quality and fatigue, while vocal attractiveness has not been tested.

lead: Straw phonation is an exercise in which a person produces voiced sound through a narrow straw or tube. It is one of several semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) exercises, which partly obstruct the mouth opening during phonation, and its use in voice training and therapy has grown over roughly two decades.[1] A scoping review of vocal training in healthy people found SOVT exercise, mainly with a tube or straw, to be the most frequently used approach in the studies it mapped.[2]

People interested in improving how their voice sounds, including singers, speakers and members of voice-improvement communities, use it as a warm-up and as a way to practise smoother, more efficient voicing. The appearance-adjacent chain proponents describe is: easier, less strained phonation, then a steadier and more resonant voice, then a voice that comes across as clearer and more confident in person and on recordings.

Research has measured its immediate effects on vocal tract and glottal function, aerodynamic and electroglottographic parameters, and its use in therapy programmes for dysphonia and vocal fatigue.[3][4][5][6] These studies address voice quality and function rather than perceived attractiveness or authority, which communities interested in voice looksmaxxing sometimes discuss.
infobox: Straw in air, straw in water (water-resistance therapy)

paras: SOVT exercises include phonating into straws or tubes, lip trills and tongue trills; much of the research has used straw phonation, and comparisons have measured the intraoral pressures of thirteen different semi-occluding gestures.[1][5]

Two main forms appear in the literature. In straw phonation in air, the person voices a sustained sound or glide through a narrow straw. In water-resistance therapy, the free end of a tube or straw is submerged in water, so the bubbling adds a pulsing pressure to the steady back pressure.[7] A 2026 scoping review of 107 studies describes straw phonation in air as a single-source system providing stable back pressure, and water-resistance therapy as a double-source system in which water depth sets hydrostatic pressure and bubbling creates pulsatile pressure of roughly 15 to 40 Hz.[7]

SOVT exercises have a long history in singing pedagogy, and the research literature describes their use for habilitation and rehabilitation of the voice as having grown substantially over the past two decades.[1] Much of the modern research and teaching vocabulary comes from voice science, including the field of vocology, a term coined by voice scientist Ingo Titze, long associated with the National Center for Voice and Speech.[8]

Speech-language pathologists, singing teachers and choir directors use straw exercises as a short warm-up or cool-down. Studies have asked, for example, whether speech-language pathologists can use straw phonation as a vocal warm-up.[9]

sections.h: How it is thought to work
paras: Proponents and researchers describe a shared mechanism: narrowing the exit of the vocal tract raises pressure above the vocal folds, which changes how the folds vibrate and can let the voice be produced with less collision force and effort. A 2026 review reports that straw phonation in air is effective at reducing mediolateral supraglottic compression and vocal fold impact stress, particularly with small-diameter straws of 3 mm or less.[7]

Imaging and aerodynamic studies in singers have measured changes in vocal tract shape and glottal function during and after the exercise, including a CT study of a single trained singer and measurements of aerodynamic and electroglottographic changes in four singers.[3][5] A laboratory study used excised canine larynges to examine how variations in a simulated straw system change aerodynamic parameters.[10]

Imaging work in a single trained singer used computed tomography to compare vocal tract and glottal measures during and after phonation into a tube and a narrow straw.[3] A prospective case series of four singers measured aerodynamic and electroglottographic changes immediately after straw phonation, lip trill and tongue trill.[5]

A study of patients with dysphonia compared three SOVT therapy programmes, lip trill, water-resistance therapy and straw phonation; its authors noted that immediate effects were well established but that the effect of multi-session programmes had been less confirmed.[4] Other studies examined immediate acoustic effects in dysphonic voices, effects on vocal fatigue, lingering effects after exercise, and a comparison of two SOVT training programmes in future occupational voice users.[6][11][12][13]

A randomised study in 27 children aged 5 to 10 with vocal cord nodules or cysts compared straw phonation with complete voice rest and reported reduced roughness and breathiness, along with improved noise measures, after about three minutes of exercise.[14] In a randomised trial of 38 adults aged 60 and over with aging-related vocal fold atrophy, a 4-week programme of straw phonation in water plus vocal hygiene was associated with improvements in glottal gap area, perceived breathiness, several acoustic and aerodynamic measures and voice-related quality-of-life scores compared with vocal hygiene alone.[15]

For vocal fatigue, a prospective study of 25 healthy participants compared 10 minutes of straw phonation with vocal rest after a one-hour vocal loading task, and a later randomised trial of 114 vocally healthy adults compared different straw-exercise regimens under simulated occupational voice loading.[11][16] A quasi-experimental study of a 48-member choir measured acoustic and self-reported effects of a four-minute straw protocol.[17]
No identified study tested straw phonation for perceived vocal attractiveness or pitch change.

In communities interested in voice improvement, straw phonation is generally discussed alongside resonance and breath-support practice as a warm-up that can be done anywhere with a drinking straw. Proponents describe it as a low-effort way to loosen up the voice before speaking or recording.

Published trials examine voice function in singers, patients and people at risk of vocal fatigue; they do not examine how listeners rate attractiveness, so the connection to a more appealing voice is a claim made by practitioners rather than a measured outcome.[2]

The reviewed studies do not report notable harms. Researchers describe the exercises as used for habilitation and rehabilitation of the voice.[1] People with a voice disorder are generally directed by clinicians to a speech-language pathologist for an individual programme.

lore.intro: Voice-improvement communities discuss straw phonation mainly as a warm-up and as a way to build easier voicing; the research behind it comes from voice therapy and singing studies.[2]
